lead: Elastic computing adds or removes running capacity as demand changes. On-demand computing means a user can ask for a resource when needed and stop paying when it is released. Together they let a cloud group follow traffic instead of buying for the worst hour. The control loop measures load, compares it with a target, and changes the number of servers inside a minimum and maximum. You meet this in web apps, batch queues and video streaming, where load rises at known times and falls later.
prereq: You need chapter 2.1 for data centre capacity, and Unit 4 for provisioning and scheduling policies.

blocks.text: Scalability is the ability of a system to grow and still work. Elasticity is automatic, demand-driven scaling inside limits. A system can be scalable but not elastic: you can add servers by hand, but nothing reacts to a traffic spike at 9 p.m. Elasticity is the control that uses scalability.

Vertical scaling changes the size of one machine. Scaling up gives a server more CPU, memory or disk; scaling down removes them. This is simple and keeps one address, but it hits a hardware ceiling and often needs a restart. Horizontal scaling changes the number of machines. Scaling out adds servers; scaling in removes them. It needs a load balancer, so see chapter 2.5.

items: On-demand capacity is started for a short period and billed by time used, such as a server-hour. A server-hour is one server running for one hour.
Reserved capacity is booked for a long period. It is cheaper per hour but paid even when idle.
An elastic group is a set of identical servers managed as one unit, with minimum and maximum size.

blocks.where: N is the number of servers (a whole number); L is peak load in requests per second (RPS); C is safe capacity per server in RPS; ceil rounds a value up to the nearest whole number; a value that is already whole stays the same, so 12 stays 12.

blocks.text: An auto-scaler is a control loop. It collects metrics, checks a rule or target, changes capacity, waits, then repeats. Metrics are measured numbers such as CPU utilisation (per cent), queue length (jobs waiting) and requests per second (RPS).

items: Collect metrics from each server and from the group.
Compare the metric with the target, for example 60% CPU.
If load is above target and size is below maximum, scale out. If load is below target and size is above minimum, scale in.
Enforce a cooldown, such as 300 s, before the next change. This is the wait after a scaling action.
Take a server from a warm pool when possible. A warm pool holds stopped servers that can start quickly.
Run a health check before sending traffic. A health check tests whether a server answers.

blocks.text: Minimum and maximum limits cap the group. The minimum keeps spare capacity for failures; the maximum protects cost and downstream systems. Some syllabi call the rule engine an automated scaling listener.

items: Target tracking keeps a metric near a set value, such as 60% CPU.
Step scaling adds a larger step when the breach is large.
Scheduled scaling changes capacity at a known time, such as a ticket sale.
Predictive scaling learns a daily pattern and adds capacity before the rise.

blocks.text: Choose a metric that moves before users suffer. CPU is easy but lags on I/O-bound work. Queue length shows backlog directly. Requests per second shows arrival rate. Pair it with latency: high latency with high CPU and high RPS means scale out; high latency with low CPU and low RPS means the bottleneck is outside the group (a slow database or downstream service), so adding servers will not help.

Flapping, or thrashing, is rapid scale out and scale in. A cooldown of 300 s after each change stops it. Average CPU can hide one hot instance. Use per-instance CPU metrics to find it; a health check only tells you whether a server responds, not whether it is overloaded. A warm pool reduces boot delay but you still pay for the storage and resources kept ready for the stopped servers.

Scale in slowly. Remove one server at a time and watch latency. If a server is unhealthy, replace it before you count it as spare. Keep logs of every scaling action: time, metric value, old size, new size and reason. Reserved capacity is not elasticity: it is a fixed booking. On-demand capacity follows the peak only when the loop has a correct target and limits.

examples.question: A web app peaks at 600 requests per second for 4 hours. Each server handles 100 requests per second at full load. The target is 60% utilisation, so each server is kept at 60 requests per second. The group keeps a minimum of 2 servers. A server-hour costs ₹9. Assume off-peak load stays below 2 × 60 = 120 requests per second, so the minimum of 2 servers is enough outside the peak. Compare the elastic cost with running 10 servers for the full 24 hours.
steps: Capacity per server at target = 100 × 0.60 = 60 requests per second.
Minimum = 2 servers, so extra servers = 10 − 2 = 8 servers.
Base cost for 2 servers for 24 h = 2 × 24 h × ₹9 = ₹432.
Extra cost for 8 servers for 4 h = 8 × 4 h × ₹9 = ₹288.
Fixed cost for 10 servers for 24 h = 10 × 24 h × ₹9 = ₹2,160.
examples.answer: The elastic group needs 10 servers at peak and costs ₹720, against ₹2,160 for 10 servers all day, so the saving is ₹1,440.
examples.check:
peak_rps = 600
full_load = 100
target = 0.60
base = 2
peak_hours = 4
rate = 9
per_server = full_load * target
required = peak_rps / per_server
extra = required - base
base_cost = base * 24 * rate
extra_cost = extra * peak_hours * rate
elastic_total = base_cost + extra_cost
fixed_total = required * 24 * rate
saving = fixed_total - elastic_total
for v in [per_server, required, extra, base_cost, extra_cost, elastic_total, fixed_total, saving]:
    print(int(v))

traps: Elasticity is not scalability: elasticity is automatic demand-driven scaling; scalability is the ability to grow.
Scale up/down changes one machine; scale out/in changes the number of machines. Mixing them loses marks.
Cooldown too short causes flapping; too long causes slow response. Cooldown does not add servers.
Average CPU can hide one hot instance. Check per-instance metrics before you scale the whole group.
Reserved capacity is cheaper per hour but paid when idle; on-demand is for short peaks. Compare total cost, not only hourly rate.

quiz.a: Elasticity is automatic addition or removal of capacity from measured demand, inside minimum and maximum limits.

quiz.q: What is a cooldown in auto-scaling?
quiz.a: A wait after a scaling action, for example 300 s, before the next action.

quiz.q: State two differences between scale up and scale out.
quiz.a: Scale up changes one machine's CPU, memory or disk; scale out changes the number of machines. Scale up often needs a restart and has a hardware ceiling; scale out needs a load balancer.

quiz.q: Why does an auto-scaler use a warm pool?
quiz.a: A warm pool holds stopped but ready servers; scale out can start them faster than a cold boot, reducing response delay.

quiz.q: Peak load is 900 RPS. Each server handles 150 RPS at full load. Target is 50% utilisation. Minimum is 3 servers. Find required servers and extra servers.
quiz.a: Capacity per server at target = 150 × 0.50 = 75 RPS. Required = ceil(900 ÷ 75) = 12 servers. Extra = 12 − 3 = 9 servers.

quiz.q: A group needs 12 servers for 3 peak hours. Base is 3 servers. A server-hour costs ₹8. Find elastic cost and saving against 12 servers for 24 h.
Average CPU is 55% but users see delays. Explain two reasons auto-scaling may fail and what to change.
quiz.a: One hot instance may be at 100% while average is low; use per-instance metrics. The metric may lag I/O wait; use queue length or latency. A long cooldown may delay scale out; shorten it or use scheduled scaling.

quiz.q: Explain flapping and how cooldown, minimum and maximum limits reduce it.
quiz.a: Flapping is rapid scale out and in as metrics cross the target. Cooldown waits after each action; minimum and maximum stop runaway changes; target tracking with a dead band also helps.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production teams use Kubernetes Horizontal Pod Autoscaler, AWS Auto Scaling and similar controllers to run the loop described here. Research looks at predictive scaling from logs and at carbon-aware scaling, where jobs run when power is cleaner. Newer curricula connect this topic with serverless concurrency and queue-based workers. Search for target tracking, cooldown, warm pool and Kubernetes Horizontal Pod Autoscaler.
